meaning: Brings up a quality or feeling and stresses how extreme it is, with a strong exclamatory tone: “talk about ...!” or “the ... was just unbelievable.”
connection: Noun (often an 「〜さ」 noun) / い-adjective or な-adjective (noun-modifying form) + こと + といったら

senses.label: Extreme degree
senses.meaning: Picks out a quality or feeling and stresses that it is far beyond normal. The second half often says “words can't describe it” or “so ... that ...”. It shows the speaker's strong emotion and works for both good and bad things.
senses.connection: Adjective turned noun with 「〜さ」 / emotion noun (「驚き」「喜び」「悲しみ」, etc.) + といったら (often followed by 「言葉にできない」 or 「〜ほどだ」)
examples: The joy I felt then was beyond words.
I'll never forget how beautiful the sunrise was from the summit.
I still remember the shock when I realized my wallet was gone.

senses.label: 〜ことといったら
senses.meaning: Here the adjective is followed directly by 「こと」 and then 「といったら」. The meaning is the same as above, but it sounds more conversational and vivid. It is often used to say someone or something is “just so ...”.
senses.connection: い-adjective dictionary form / な-adjective + な + ことといったら
examples: His room is so filthy there's nowhere to even step.
Newborn babies are so cute, I could watch them forever.
The forest at night was so quiet I could hear my own heartbeat.

senses.label: Leaving the rest unsaid
senses.meaning: Only the first half is said, and the evaluation is left out. The tone alone says “I can't even describe it.” Common in speech and in dialogue in novels. In casual speech, 「〜ことったら」 is also used.
senses.connection: 〜さ／〜こと + といったら……／ったら！ (ends with 「……」 or 「！」)
examples: Oh, the embarrassment when I fell in front of everyone...

notes: The second half must be a strong exclamation or an expression of very high degree; a flat, neutral description will not do. ✕「その美しさといったら、きれいだった」→ ○「その美しさといったら、言葉にできないほどだった」.

It is most easily confused with the topic-raising 「〜といったら」: 「日本の夏といったら花火だ」 only means “when you say Japanese summer, you think of fireworks”, with no exclamation about degree. It is this pattern only when 「〜さ」 or an emotion noun comes before it and an evaluation of degree follows.
A common mistake is in the connection: an adjective must be nominalized first. ✕「うれしいといったら」→ ○「うれしさといったら」 or 「うれしいことといったら」; な-adjectives take 「な」: ○「静かなことといったら」.

It carries strong emotion and the speaker's subjective exaggeration, so it is out of place in formal reports or business writing. Used about someone else's faults (e.g. 「部長のしつこさといったら」), it sounds like grumbling, and saying it to the person themselves or to a superior is very rude.
The contracted 「〜ことったら」 is very casual; use it only with people you are close to, never with elders or clients.

daily.title: Telling stories after a trip
daily.description: Describing amazing scenery to a friend and stressing how impressive it was.
daily.example: That waterfall was so powerful. Photos don't capture it at all.

daily.title: Complaining to family
daily.description: Grumbling to family that someone or something was way too much.
daily.example: The neighbor's dog was so loud, I couldn't sleep all night.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character recalls the past, and the pattern heightens a strong emotion.
daily.example: The grief of losing my mother was truly beyond words.

work.title: Award acceptance speech
work.description: At an awards ceremony or company recognition event, expressing the joy of winning.
work.example: I still remember the joy I felt when I heard I had won.

work.title: Magazines and essays
work.description: Food and travel columns use it to stress how great an experience was.
work.example: The ramen here is so delicious, no wonder people line up for it.

etymology: Made from the particle 「と」 + 「言ったら」, the conditional of 「言う」. The original meaning is “if we talk about ...”. From the idea “once you start talking about it, you can't stop (or can't find the words)”, it came to be an exclamation stressing degree. In 「ことといったら」, 「こと」 is a formal noun that turns the adjective into a noun.

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: The closest in origin and meaning: both stress “extremely ...”. 「〜といったらない」 fixes the conclusion as “indescribable” and closes the sentence by itself (e.g. 「悔しいといったらない」); this pattern only puts the subject forward first, and the second half can freely continue with 「〜ほどだ」, 「言葉にできない」 and so on, or be left out.

similar.title: 〜ことか
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning, also expressing how deep a feeling is, but it comes at the end of the sentence and often pairs with 「どんなに」 or 「何度」: 「どんなに心配したことか」. This pattern instead raises the quality or feeling as a topic at the start and describes its degree in the second half.

similar.title: 〜といったら (bringing up a topic)
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「と＋言ったら」) and identical in form but different in meaning: the topic-raising use is followed by the typical thing that comes to mind (「日本の山といったら富士山だ」) in a calm tone, whereas this pattern is followed by a strong feeling or evaluation.

similar.title: 〜といえば
similar.explanation: Same origin (「と＋言えば」). It is used when one topic reminds you of something else, in a calm tone, and cannot express the exclamation “extremely ...”. Here the preceding part is a quality noun such as 「〜さ」, and the focus is on degree.

formation: Built from 「と」 (the quoting particle) + 「言ったら」 (the ta-form of 「言う」 + the conditional 「たら」), literally “if one starts talking about ...”. A quality or feeling (「うれしさ」「美しさ」) is put forward as the thing to be “talked about”, and the idea is that once you try to put it into words, the second half naturally says “there's no end to it” or “it's so extreme that ...”, which gives the exclamatory sense of “just unbelievably ...”. Because something is being brought up as a topic, a noun must come before it: an adjective becomes 「〜さ」, or is nominalized with the formal noun 「こと」 to make 「〜ことといったら」. And since the second half only says what you would find if you did talk about it, it is often dropped altogether, leaving 「〜といったら……」, with the trailing tone doing the work of “I can't even describe it”.
